think.q: What does "declarative" mean in React?
opts: You describe what the UI should be for the current state; React handles the DOM steps
You write every DOM change step by step
why: The opposite, imperative code, says how: find, change, append, remove.

think.q: Which problem is React best at solving?
opts: Making a static brochure page load faster
Keeping a complex, frequently changing UI in sync with data
why: For a mostly static page, plain HTML (or a framework that ships less JS) is often the better fit.

think.q: React itself is…
opts: A full framework with routing and a server
A library for building UI components; routing, data fetching and builds come from other tools or frameworks
why: That is why Next.js, React Router and TanStack Query exist.

think.q: How does data flow in React?
opts: Both ways automatically, like two-way binding
Down from parent to child through props; children ask parents to change things through callbacks
From child to parent through props
why: One-way flow makes it easy to find who owns a piece of data.

try.task: Feel the idea without React: write renderTodos(todos), a pure function that returns the HTML string for a list, plus a "N left" line. Same input → same output, no DOM access.
try.hint: map over todos, join, and count the not-done ones. This is exactly what a component does, minus JSX.

checks.t: done items get a class and are not counted
same input gives the same output

takeaway.key: UI = f(state). Describe the screen for the current state; React updates the DOM to match.
mistakes: Thinking React is a full framework.
Using React for a page that barely changes.

opts: Makes el the root React manages and renders App into it
why: Everything inside that element now belongs to React.

think.q: Why does npm run build exist when npm run dev already works?

dryRun.title: <Badge count={120} />
dryRun.note: A component is a function that takes props and returns JSX (or null to render nothing). Names start with a capital letter, so JSX knows it is a component and not an HTML tag.

think.q:
function badge({ n }) { return <b>{n}</b> }
function Badge({ n }) { return <b>{n}</b> }
why: Lowercase JSX tags are treated as HTML elements, so <badge> becomes an unknown DOM element and the function is never called.

think.q:
function Empty() { return null }
function Zero() { return 0 }
function No() { return false }
why: null and false render nothing; the number 0 is rendered as text.

think.q: function Title({ text }) { return <h1>{text.toUpperCase()}</h1> }
why: A missing prop is undefined, and calling a method on it throws during render.

think.q: Why can a component not return two sibling elements like <h1/><p/> directly?
opts: JSX must have one parent; wrap them in a Fragment <>…</>
React forbids two elements per component
why: A component returns one value; a Fragment groups children without adding a DOM node.

think.q: A component should behave like a pure function. What does that mean here?
opts: Same props and state → same JSX, with no side effects during render
why: Side effects (fetching, timers, DOM writes) go in event handlers or effects.

try.task: Write Badge({ count }): render nothing for 0 (or less), the number for 1–99, and "99+" above 99, inside <span aria-label="notifications">.
try.hint: Return null early for count <= 0. Use a ternary for the label.

takeaway.key: A component is a capitalised function: props in, JSX out. Return null to render nothing; keep render pure.

think.q: Why does { if (ok) <p/> } inside JSX fail?
opts: if is not allowed in components
Curly braces take expressions only; use a ternary, &&, or compute before the return

think.q: How does a child tell its parent that something happened?
opts: The parent passes a function prop (onSelect), and the child calls it
The child changes the parent's props
The child sets a global variable
why: Data goes down as props; events go up as callback props.

think.q: What is the risk of <Input {...props} />?
opts: Unknown props end up on the DOM element (warnings) or override what you set before the spread
why: Destructure what you use and spread the rest deliberately, in the right order.

dryRun.title: Clicking "+2" which calls setCount(count + 1) twice
dryRun.note: State is a component's memory. Calling the setter schedules a re-render; the value in the current render does not change. When the next value depends on the previous one, use the updater form: setCount(c => c + 1).

think.q:
function C() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0)
  return <button onClick={() => { setN(n + 1); setN(n + 1) }}>{n}</button>
}
why: Both calls read n from the same render (0), so both set 1.

think.q:
function C() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0)
  return <button onClick={() => { setN((x) => x + 1); setN((x) => x + 1) }}>{n}</button>
}
why: Updaters are queued and each receives the latest value.

think.q:
function C() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0)
  return <button onClick={() => { setN(n + 5); console.log('inside', n) }}>{n}</button>
}
why: The setter does not change the variable in the running code; the new value appears in the next render.

think.q:
function L() {
  const [list, setList] = useState(['a'])
  return <button onClick={() => { list.push('b'); setList(list) }}>{list.length}</button>
}
why: Same array reference → React sees no change and skips the re-render. Always create a new array/object: setList([...list, "b"]).

think.q: Which data should NOT be state?
opts: A value you can compute from props or other state, like a filtered list
why: Derive it during render; duplicate state drifts out of sync.

try.task: Write Counter({ step = 1 }) with buttons "−", "+" and "+ twice" (adds step two times using the updater form), a "Reset" button, and the value in <output>.
try.hint: useState(0); setCount(c => c + step) twice for "+ twice".

tests.code:
import { render, screen, fireEvent } from '@testing-library/react'
import { expect, test } from 'vitest'
import { Counter } from './Counter'

const value = () => screen.getByRole('status').textContent

test('adds and subtracts by step', () => {
  render(<Counter step={5} />)
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('+'))
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('+'))
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('−'))
  expect(value()).toBe('5')
})

test('+ twice really adds two steps', () => {
  render(<Counter step={5} />)
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('+ twice'))
  expect(value()).toBe('10')
})

test('reset goes back to 0', () => {
  render(<Counter />)
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('+'))
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('Reset'))
  expect(value()).toBe('0')
})

takeaway.key: setState schedules a re-render; the current value does not change. Use updaters for "based on previous", and always replace (never mutate) arrays and objects.
mistakes: Mutating an array then setting the same reference.
